body.p: As of the pending Office Action, claims 1-34 are pending and stand rejected. Claims 1, 2, 7, 8, 12-16, 24, 28, and 30-33 are amended herein. Claim 29 is canceled and new dependent claim 35 added. No new matter is being added.

By making these amendments, Applicant is not conceding that the claims originally presented were not patentable over the cited references. Applicant reserves the right to pursue patentability of the original claims and/or any other claims supported by the present application in one or more continuing applications.
Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the application in view of the foregoing amendments and the remarks appearing below.
Claims 1-34 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as allegedly being indefinite for
failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor regards as the invention. Applicant respectfully disagrees.

Claims 1, 12, 16, 24, and 28-32 are said to be indefinite because it is unclear how the device is configured to monitor "because there is no positively recited configured monitoring, sensing or performing a similar activity." There is no basis in law or rule for this rejection and none is cited in the office action. A claim is definite if a person of ordinary skill understands the subject matter of the claim with a reasonable degree of clarity and particularity when read in light of the specification and teachings of the prior art. MPEP 2173.02(II). For example, see In re Larsen, 10 Fed. App'x 890 (Fed. Cir. 2001) (The preamble of the Larsen claim recited only a hanger and a loop but the body of the claim positively recited a linear member. The court observed that the totality of all the limitations of the claim and their interaction with each other must be considered to ascertain the inventor's contribution to the art. Upon review of the claim in its entirety, the court concluded that the claim at issue apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope and, therefore, serves the notice function required by 35 U.S.C. 112.). When read in light of the present specification, there is no possibility that a person of ordinary skill does not understand the scope of the claim. This rejection is made in error and should be withdrawn.

With respect to claim 23, relative terminology as used is not per se indefinite as appears to be suggested in the rejection. As stated in MPEP 2173.05: "Acceptability of [relative terminology in] the claim language depends on whether one of ordinary skill in the art would understand what is claimed, in light of the specification." In this case, the limitation recited in claim 23 is explained in depth in specification [0121]. On the basis of this description, a person of ordinary skill would clearly understand that the claimed range of "about 0.05N-0.3N" would encompass minor variations that did not change the function or operational characteristics of the device.

Claim 32 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(d) as allegedly being in improper dependent form for failing to further limit the subject matter of the claim upon which it depends, or for failing to include all the limitations of the claim upon which it depends. Applicant respectfully disagrees.

Claim 32 as previously presented limited the "at least one loop" recited in claim 25 to be "a single loop", thus narrowing the claimed invention by eliminating combinations with more than one loop. Claim 32 is now amended which also eliminates the basis for this rejection.

Claims 1-4, 7-10, 12, 16-17, 21, 28 and 30 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) as allegedly being anticipated by U.S. Patent Publication No. 2006/0178695 to Decant et al. ("Decant"). Applicant respectfully disagrees.

There is no reasonable interpretation of Decant in which the legs (10, 12, 14, 16, 18, and 20) of the disclosed vena cava filter joined by single wire conductors form a multistranded, variable inductance coil. The statement in the office action that "the inductance coil is made up of the elements it comprises" does not change the fact that there is no coil. The mere fact that a group of elements may form a circle, does not make those elements into a variable inductance coil - which is a specific term of art with a specific meaning understood by persons of ordinary skill.

The claims also recite that the variable inductance coil is formed around an open center. Again, there is no reasonable interpretation of the vena cava filter cited in the office action as having an open center. The legs of the vena cava filter that are asserted to be part of the coil in

Decant are all joined together at the center of the device. While there is no end view of the embodiment of Fig. 1A cited, an end view of that embodiment would look like the following annotated Fig. 5A.

Claim 1 is also amended herein to recite a flexible sensor frame formed in an open center loop and that the plurality of wire strands are wrapped on the flexible sensor frame around the open center. This structure is very clearly not disclosed or suggested by the vena cava filters disclosed in Decant. It is to be noted that the conductive bridges 26 of Decant cannot at once be both strands of the coil and the separate flexible frame on which the coil is disposed.
Claim 2 is amended herein to clarify that the plural wire strands arranged around the open center extend around the open center. Again, there is no such structure disclosed in Decant.

Claim 7 is amended to further specify that each individual strand of the plurality of strands is individually insulated and that further all of the strands and the sensor frame are covered together by an outer layer. This structure is not shown in Decant and a covering over all of the components that the Examiner asserts to comprise the coil in Decant, it would occlude the vessel in which it is placed.

Claim 8 is amended to specify that the plurality of wire strands fully surround the flexible sensor frame. This structure is shown in FIGS. 2 and 2A (cross-sectional views) of the present application. No such structure is disclosed in Decant.

With respect to claim 10, the Examiner asserts that vena cava legs (10, 12, 14, 16, 18, and 20) comprise the recited "plural-side-by-side strands", yet those strands are not formed in a continuous loop. The conductive bridges 26 do not cause the legs of the vena cava filter to be formed in a continuous loop.
Claim 12 is amended herein to recite "a flexible sensor frame comprising a flexible

elongate member formed into a loop and joined together at opposite ends to form an open center surrounded by the flexible elongate member" and that the coil comprised of plural wire strands is formed on the flexible sensor frame. There is no such structure disclosed in Decant.

Claim 16 is amended herein to recite the wire strands of the coil as being "twisted into bundles with said bundles forming at least one loop around the open center." This structure is described, for example, in para [0080] of the present application (as published). There are no bundles of twisted wire strands disclosed in Decant.

Claim 17 requires "each of said wire stands" to be in side-by-side contact with plural other wire strands. According to the Examiner, conductive bridges 26 are wire strands of the variable inductance coil asserted to be disclosed by Decant. However, the conductive bridges 26 are quite clearly not in side-by-side contact with any other alleged wire strand in the Decant vena cava filter.

Claim 28 recites the coil as "comprising at least one bundle of wire strands". A wire strand bundle has a specific meaning in arts related to coils used as electronic circuit elements describing a collection of multiple wire strands (often twisted together) which are then disposed in a loop to form the coil. Persons skilled in the art understand this meaning. It is also described in the present application at paras. [0080], [0123] and [0124]. The legs of the Decant vena cava filter combined with conductive bridges would not be understood by persons skilled in the art to be a bundle of wire strands as claimed. Further claim 28 is amended herein to further recite a flexible sensor on which the at least one bundle of wire strand is disposed. No such frame with a bundle of wire strands disposed thereon is disclosed in Decant. Amended claim 28 further recites that the bundle of wire strands is in contact with the flexible sensor frame "all around the open center." This structure, which is shown in the present application in FIGS. 2, 2A, 21A, and 21B among others, is not present in Decant.
Claim 30 is amended herein to clarify that the plurality of wire strands of the coil are
twisted together and make at least one turn around the open center of the coil. No such structure is disclosed in Decant.
For the foregoing reasons, Decant does not anticipate any claims of the present application and withdrawal of this rejection is respectfully requested.

Claims 5, 11, and 18 are said to be rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over U.S. Patent Publication No. 2017/0216508 to Zilbershlag et al. ("Zilbershlag"). Based on the explanation of this rejection, Applicant believes that the correct statement of the rejection is as unpatentable over Decant in view of Zilbershlag, and the rejection will be addressed as such. Applicant respectfully disagrees.

The Examiner misstates the teaching of Zilbershlag regarding the use of biocompatible coverings. Nowhere does Zilbershlag state that the addition of a covering material improves biocompatibility of the device as asserted by the Examiner. All that Zilbershlag says is that the covering around the inductive wires is "preferably biocompatible." See para [0151]. As Zilbershlag discloses copper wire as one of the materials for the implanted coil (para [0054], it would be expected by a person skilled in the art that the copper wire would be provided with a biocompatible covering. However, in contrast to Zilbershlag, and as previously recognized by the Examiner, Decant discloses that the legs of the vena cava filter are to be made from "metals or metal alloys (e.g., nitinol) that are well known to one of ordinary skill in the art for implantation within a blood vessel." Decant, para. [0054]. There would be no reason for a person skilled in the art to provide a biocompatible covering over a material that is specifically selected for biocompatibility and human body implantation. There is thus no basis for the proposed combination and this rejection should be withdrawn.
In addition to the foregoing lack of motivation to combine, these claims are also patentable based on their dependency from patentable independent claims.

Regarding claims 19 and 20, although not included in the statement of the rejection, it appears that these claims are also rejected over the combination of Decant and Zilbershlag. In rejecting claims 19 and 20, the Examiner asserts that FIG. 18A of Decant shows plural adjacent wire strands wrapped plural times around the open center. However, there is no open center of
the device shown in FIG. 18A. Further, there is no reasonable interpretation of the structure shown as having the legs 4 wrapped multiple times around anything.
Claims 6 and 22 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Decant in view of U.S. Patent No. 3,838,683 to Kolin ("Kolin"). Applicant respectfully disagrees.

The Examiner states that a person skilled in the art would be motivated to modify Decant by the teachings of Kolin "because modifying the device to be collapsible would help facilitate percutaneous introduction, as recognized by Kolin." However, Decant is already designed to be collapsible without the teachings of Kolin: "The legs are configured with materials such that they may be collapsed toward a central axis along the length of the device for insertion and/or retrieval from a patient's vascular system." Decant, para. 0054. There is thus no reason to modify Decant as asserted and this rejection should be withdrawn for that reason.
In addition to the foregoing lack of motivation to combine, these claims are also patentable based on their dependency from patentable independent claims.
Claims 13-15, 29, and 31 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being
unpatentable over Decant in view of U.S Patent Publication No. 2008/0033527 to Nunez et al. ("Nunez"). Applicant respectfully disagrees.

The rejection of these claims is based on the assertion that the legs 4 and conductive bridges 26 of Decant form the recited coil. The proposed modification of Decant to meet the limitations of claim 13-15 would then require that the legs of the vena cava filter be wrapped onto a frame. The legs of Decant are straight and specifically configured for the purpose of forming a filter basket to capture particles and to sense the capture of particle as a result of strain induced in the legs when particles are captured. [0056]. This modification would render Decant inoperable for its intended purpose and is thus improperly made. If instead the modification intended by the Examiner is to wrap wire strands 422 of Nunez onto the legs 4 of Decant, then that contradicts the rejection anticipation rejection above in which it is asserted that the legs 4 form the recited coil. In either case, the proposed modification does not meet the claim language.
Further, the supposed motivation to "predictably help the device be suitable for

implanting within an injured or diseased blood vessel, as recognized by Nunez" is neither a teaching of Nunez nor relevant to Decant. The Examiner asserts that this teaching is provided in para [0069], but the wire strands 422 are not discussed there. Moreover, the wire strands are disclosed in para [0069] as being provided to form an inductive coil for purposes of powering other sensors via inductive power coupling. Wires 422 have nothing to do with making the devices suitable for implantation in an injured or diseased vessel.
In addition to the foregoing reasons, these claims are also patentable based on their dependency from patentable independent claims.

Claim 23 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Decant in view of Kolin, as applied to claim 22, and further in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2013/0245745 to Vong et al. ("Vong"). Applicant respectfully disagrees.

Claim 23, via claims 21 and 22, is limited to a device configured and dimensioned to be implanted in a patient's IVC. Vong is not described as being implanted in the IVC and therefore a person skilled in the art would not consider the teachings of Vong as relevant due to the substantially different physiology of the IVC compared with other vessels, in particular with the carotid artery, which is mentioned a number of times as the placement location for the Vong device. There is thus no basis for combining the references as proposed.
In addition to the foregoing lack of motivation to combine, these claims are also patentable based on their dependency from patentable independent claims.
Claims 24-26 and 32-33 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being
unpatentable over Decant in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2010/0076543 to Melsheimer et al. ("Melsheimer"). Applicant respectfully disagrees.
For the reasons stated above, Decant does not disclose an expandable and collapsible coil comprising a plurality of wire strands and the rejection is made in error for this reason alone.

Additionally Melsheimer does not disclose or suggest wire strands twisted together into plural bundles with said bundles wrapped together to form a coil as recited in amended claim 24. The rejection is also overcome for this reason.

Claim 25 recites a resonant circuit with the collapsible coil as a component thereof. The wire strands 12 of Melsheimer are structural members, not elements of an electric circuit. A person of ordinary skill would not consider such structures as relevant to providing an inductance coil in a resonant circuit.

Further, the motivation to combine these references as stated in the office action does not match the actual disclosure of the references. Nowhere does Melsheimer say that the use of filaments 12 improve flexibility. Increased flexibility is mentioned in Melsheimer in only one place - para [0050] - and there it is attributed to the overall design of the disclosed stent with a plurality of rows created by spiral formation.
For these reasons, this rejection is made in error and should be withdrawn.

Claim 27 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Decant in view of Melsheimer, as applied to claim 25, and further in view of WO 2006/125215 to Gray et al. ("Gray"). Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Claim 27 is at least patentable based on its dependency from patentable claims as above.

Claim 34 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Decant in view of Melsheimer, as applied to claim 25, and further in view of Non-Patent Literature titled "Inductance calculation of planar multi-layer and multi-wire coils: An analytical approach" by Christian Peters et al. ("Peters"). Applicant respectfully disagrees.

Melsheimer discloses nothing at all related to electrical properties of inductance coils and nothing related to the use of inductance coils. Peters is directed to specific configurations of inductance coils. There is no reason a person of ordinary skill would modify the structural wire configurations of Melsheimer according to the teachings about electrical properties of inductance coils in Peters. The only possible way this combination was made is based on a hindsight reconstruction of references specially selected without regard for their actual teachings. This rejection is made in error and should be withdrawn.
In addition to the foregoing lack of motivation to combine, these claims are also patentable based on their dependency from patentable independent claims.
Applicant submits that all pending claims are in condition for allowance and so

allowance thereof is respectfully requested. Applicant's amendment of the claims does not constitute a concession that the claims are not allowable in their unamended form.
